title: East and west both belong to Allah.
subtitle: When people mock you for changing direction
then: In Madinah the Muslims had prayed toward Bayt Al-Maqdis for about sixteen or seventeen months. When the command came to face the Ka'bah, some people said: {trap}what is wrong with them, facing one way and then another?{/trap} The verse answers before the question even spreads: {idea}east and west belong to Allah.{/idea}
now: You start praying again, or stop a habit your friends still enjoy. Someone in the family group chat says, "So now you are religious?" The change looks strange from outside. {idea}You did not switch sides. You followed the One who owns every direction.{/idea}
old: If I change my ways, people will see me as unstable.
new: Changing to follow Allah is not instability. It is the most stable thing I can do.
try: Think of one good change you made that someone questioned. Thank Allah for it quietly tonight.

title: No prayer offered in obedience is ever wasted.
subtitle: A middle community, a test, and a mercy
then: Some Muslims had died before the Qiblah changed, and the believers worried about their prayers toward Jerusalem. {reward}Allah would never make your faith be lost.{/reward} The same verse calls them a just, middle community, and says the change was {trap}heavy except for those Allah guided.{/trap}
now: You prayed for years with little knowledge. Now you learn more and a quiet voice says, "All those years did not count." Or your late grandmother practised as she knew how. {reward}Sincere obedience with what you knew is not erased by learning more.{/reward}
old: Everything I did before I knew better was worthless.
new: Allah keeps what I gave Him sincerely, and the test is whether I follow now.
try: Make a short dua for someone who died before you could teach or learn from them more.

title: Allah saw him looking up at the sky.
subtitle: A silent longing that was answered
then: The Prophet ﷺ prayed toward Bayt Al-Maqdis as commanded, yet he loved the Qiblah of Ibrahim. He would supplicate and keep looking up at the sky, {idea}waiting for Allah's command{/idea} rather than changing it himself. Then came: {reward}We have seen the turning of your face.{/reward}
now: There is a wish you have not told anyone. A job, a child, a healing, a way out. You look up at the ceiling at night more than you admit. {reward}The verse says your silent looking up is seen.{/reward} Keep asking, and keep obeying while you wait.
old: If I do not say it out loud, no one knows what I long for.
new: Allah sees even the turning of my face before I speak.
try: Tonight, look up and name your quiet wish to Allah in one sentence.

title: No sign moves a heart set on its desire.
subtitle: Why more proof does not always help
then: The People of the Scripture knew the truth, yet Ibn Kathir says {trap}no proof would make them abandon their desires.{/trap} Then the warning is aimed at the Prophet ﷺ and his community: following others' wishes {idea}after knowledge has come{/idea} is wrongdoing, because the proof against one who knows is stronger.
now: You know the facts about a habit. The article, the doctor's warning, the ayah. You still scroll past it, waiting for one more proof. {trap}The problem was never missing evidence.{/trap} {idea}Knowing more makes your choice weigh more.{/idea}
old: If I just had more proof, I would change.
new: When desire is in charge, proof is never enough. What I already know is my test.
try: Pick one thing you already know is right and do the first small step today.

title: They knew him like they knew their own sons.
subtitle: Hiding what you clearly recognize
then: The Arabs used knowing your own child as a picture of something {idea}completely obvious.{/idea} Ibn Kathir reports that 'Abdullah bin Salam, a scholar of the Israelites who became Muslim, said he recognized the Prophet ﷺ like that and even more. Yet {trap}a party hid the truth while knowing it.{/trap}
now: At work you know whose idea it really was. In the family you know who was actually wrong in the fight. Staying quiet is easier. {trap}Hiding what you clearly know is its own act.{/trap} {idea}Saying it, gently, is the honest choice.{/idea}
old: If I stay quiet about what I know, I have done nothing wrong.
new: Hiding a truth I recognize as clearly as my own child is a choice I will answer for.
try: Give credit today to someone whose good work you know went unnoticed.

title: The truth is from your Lord. Do not doubt.
subtitle: Steadying the heart after others deny
then: After describing those who mocked the change and those who hid what they knew, Allah {idea}strengthens the resolve of the Prophet ﷺ and the believers.{/idea} What came to him is {reward}the truth without doubt.{/reward}
now: You read a clever post online that makes your faith feel shaky. The comments pile on. Your certainty starts to depend on who sounds louder. {idea}The truth does not get its strength from the comment section.{/idea}
old: If enough people question it, maybe it is not true.
new: Truth is measured by its source, not by how many argue with it.
try: Next time doubt comes from a post, close it and read one ayah slowly instead.

title: Stop arguing about direction. Race to do good.
subtitle: Everyone faces somewhere; all are gathered
then: Ibn 'Abbas said this speaks of the followers of different religions: {idea}each has a direction it faces.{/idea} Allah's answer is not more debate but {reward}hasten toward all that is good.{/reward} Wherever people are scattered, Allah is able to bring them all together.
now: The argument in the comments has run three days. Nobody is changing their mind. Meanwhile the neighbour needs a lift and the charity box is empty. {idea}The verse moves you off the debate floor and onto the race track.{/idea}
old: I have to win this argument first.
new: My time is better spent getting ahead in good than getting ahead in debate.
try: Leave one online argument unanswered and do one good deed in that time instead.

title: Wherever you set out from, face the same House.
subtitle: A command repeated so the heart settles

row.title: Allah sees
sub: not unaware of what you do

row.title: now
sub: it is the truth from Me

then: This is the second time the command is given. Ibn Kathir explains each repetition adds something: first Allah granted what the Prophet ﷺ wished for, and here He states {idea}it is also the truth from Him{/idea} that He loves. It ends with a reminder: {reward}Allah is not unaware of what you do.{/reward}
now: You travel for work, move cities, change jobs. The coffee shop changes, the commute changes, the people around you change. {idea}One thing stays fixed: the direction your heart turns.{/idea} Wherever you set out from, it is the same House.
old: When life moves me around, my faith moves around with it.
new: Wherever I start from, I have one fixed point to turn toward.
try: Next time you are somewhere new, find the Qiblah first and pause facing it for a moment.

title: Fear them not. Fear Me.
subtitle: When critics will talk no matter what
then: The third repetition. Facing the Ka'bah removed the argument that the Muslims were only following another people's Qiblah. Yet {trap}those bent on wrong would still argue.{/trap} So Allah says: do not fear the doubts they raise, {idea}fear Me alone{/idea}, so that I may {reward}complete My favor upon you.{/reward}
now: You change something for Allah and brace for the remarks. Some people will understand. {trap}Some will find a complaint whatever you do.{/trap} Their voices take up your evenings. {idea}You cannot satisfy them. You only have to stand right with Allah.{/idea}
old: I need to answer every critic before I can feel at peace.
new: Some critics will never be satisfied. Fear of Allah is the only fear that settles me.
try: Name one person whose opinion you fear too much. Ask Allah to free your heart from it.

title: A messenger from among you, teaching what you never knew.
subtitle: The biggest favor in the chain of favors

row.title: purifies
sub: from the ills of the soul

then: Just as Allah completed His favor with the Qiblah, He had already given a greater one: {reward}a Messenger ﷺ from among themselves.{/reward} Ibn Kathir says he cleansed them of the worst behavior of Jahiliyyah, when {trap}they used to utter foolish statements{/trap}, and raised them to deep knowledge.
now: Think of the things you know today that you did not know at fifteen. How to pray. How to seek forgiveness. Why kindness to parents matters. {reward}Someone carried that to you, link by link, from him ﷺ.{/reward}
old: What I know about my faith is just what I grew up with.
new: Everything good I know traces back to a gift Allah sent among people like me.
try: Send a short thank you message to someone who first taught you something about Islam.

title: Remember Me and I will remember you.
subtitle: The smallest exchange with the largest return
then: After listing His favors, Allah asks for remembrance and gratitude. Ibn Kathir cites the authentic hadith: {reward}whoever mentions Me to himself, I mention him to Myself; whoever mentions Me in a gathering, I mention him in a better one.{/reward} And {idea}be grateful to Me and do not deny Me.{/idea}
now: You are stuck in traffic, or in the hospital waiting room, phone at 8 percent. You whisper "Alhamdulillah" and nobody hears. {reward}The Lord of everything mentions you in return.{/reward} One small word, a remembrance from Him back.
old: My little dhikr in the car does not really matter.
new: When I remember Allah, even quietly, He remembers me.
try: Pick one daily wait, like the kettle or a red light, and say one dhikr there.
